title: Not the Ways of Egypt or Canaan
summary: God calls Israel to live by his statutes rather than the customs of Egypt, which they have left, or of Canaan, which they are about to enter. He forbids sexual relations with close relatives, adultery, relations during menstruation, the offering of children to Molech, sexual relations between men, and bestiality. The land itself, he warns, is defiled by these practices and will vomit out any people, Canaanite or Israelite, who do them.
story: The Holiness Code, begun in chapter 17, now turns from the altar to the household. Israel stands between two worlds: Egypt behind them and Canaan ahead. Having been rescued from one and promised the other, they are told they must belong to neither. The chapter is framed by the words "I am the LORD your God" (verses 2 and 30), which recall the opening of the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20. The laws that follow are not an arbitrary list but the shape of life for a people who belong to this God. Chapter 20 will return to many of the same acts and attach penalties to them; chapter 18 states the principles.
historical:
As with the rest of Leviticus, the laws are presented as given at Sinai before Israel entered Canaan, and scholars differ on when they were written down (see the notes on chapters 16 and 17). The chapter's claim that the land had become defiled by its inhabitants draws on a theme found as early as Genesis 15:16, where God tells Abraham that the sin of the Amorites is not yet complete. Later biblical writers read the Babylonian exile through this chapter's warning: the land vomited out Israel as it had the nations before them.

Other ancient law collections also restricted marriage between close relatives. The Code of Hammurabi, from Babylon in the eighteenth century BC, punished certain forms of incest, and the Hittite laws of Anatolia prohibited some unions and forms of bestiality while permitting others. Egyptian royal families at times married brother to sister. The name Molech is associated elsewhere in the Old Testament with the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7) and with child sacrifice at a site called Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Scholars debate whether Molech was the name of a god or, as the German scholar Otto Eissfeldt argued in 1935 from Punic inscriptions in North Africa, the name of a type of sacrifice. Either way, the practice condemned is the ritual killing of children.
cultural:
Ancient Israelite households were large and close. Several generations of a family, with wives married in from other clans, might live in one compound. The incest laws protected everyone in that house: they made it safe for a girl to grow up near her uncles and cousins and for a widow to live near her husband's brothers. The repeated Hebrew phrase behind the BSB's having sexual relations, literally to uncover the nakedness of someone, was a frank idiom, and the reasons given are often about honor and relationship: to take your father's wife dishonors your father; your aunt is your father's close relative. The laws are addressed to men, the heads of households, because they held the power to abuse it.

Some of these unions had happened in Israel's own history. Abraham married his half-sister Sarah (Genesis 20:12), Jacob married two sisters, and Amram married his father's sister Jochebed and became the father of Moses (Exodus 6:20). The chapter does not comment on those ancestors, but it marks a clear break: what was once tolerated is now forbidden to the covenant people. These laws remained active centuries later. John the Baptist told Herod Antipas that it was not lawful to have his brother's wife (Mark 6:18), and Paul was appalled that a Corinthian Christian had his father's wife (1 Corinthians 5:1). In the 1520s Henry VIII of England appealed to the related law in Leviticus 20:21 to seek an annulment of his marriage to his brother's widow.
literary: The chapter has a clear frame. Verses 1 to 5 and 24 to 30 are exhortation, speaking to the whole people about Egypt, Canaan, the land, and God's statutes. Between them, verses 6 to 23 give the laws in a steady, repetitive form: "You must not" followed by a relationship and, often, a reason. The list begins with the closest relatives (mother, father's wife, sister) and moves outward to in-laws and extended family, then to acts outside the family entirely. The refrain "I am the LORD" appears at key points (verses 2, 4, 5, 6, 21, 30), grounding every law in God's name rather than in custom. Verse 5 states the promise at the heart of the chapter: "the man who does these things will live by them."

outline.t: Not the practices of Egypt or Canaan, but God's statutes
Other forbidden acts, including child sacrifice to Molech
The land that vomits out its inhabitants

doctrines.note: The chapter treats the family as a place that must be kept safe. By drawing clear lines around sexual relations, it protects the vulnerable members of a household and preserves the bonds between generations and siblings.

Holiness means being different from the surrounding nations, not by withdrawing from ordinary life but by living it under God's word. Sexual conduct is not a private matter set apart from worship; it belongs to the life of a holy people.

God's statutes are given as the path of life (verse 5), not merely as restrictions. The law describes what flourishing looks like for a people rescued by God, and Paul later uses this verse to contrast life by the law with life by faith.

The land's vomiting out of its inhabitants shows that God's judgment is impartial. The Canaanites are not condemned for being Canaanites, and Israel will receive the same judgment if it does the same things.

words.note: Ervah, nakedness. It occurs twenty-four times in this chapter. To uncover someone's nakedness is a euphemism for sexual relations, but the word also carries a sense of shame and exposure. The laws present sexual wrongdoing as exposing and dishonoring a person, often a relative whose honor is bound up with one's own.

Galah, to uncover. The same Hebrew root also means to go into exile, to be stripped from one's land. The overlap is a feature of the language rather than a hidden message, but readers have noticed that a chapter about uncovering nakedness ends by warning that the land will expel its people.

To'evah, abomination: something detestable, abhorrent to God or to a community. It is used here for the whole group of practices (verses 26, 27, 29, 30) as well as for verse 22. Elsewhere it describes idolatry, dishonest scales (Proverbs 11:1), and pride, so it is not a technical term for sexual sin alone.

Qo, to vomit. The image is startling and physical: the land is like a body that cannot hold what poisons it. The land is not a neutral piece of real estate but God's, and it responds to how people live on it.

christ: Paul quotes verse 5 twice. In Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12 he cites "The man who does these things will live by them" to describe righteousness by the law, and sets it beside the righteousness that comes by faith. His point is not that the law was bad but that no one has kept it fully, and that "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). Christ is the one who did these things and lived. Jesus also taught about marriage by going back to creation, to the man and woman made to become one flesh (Matthew 19:4-6), which is the pattern the laws of this chapter protect. And the New Testament holds out hope to people whose past includes the acts named here: after a list of sins in 1 Corinthians 6, Paul writes, "And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified" (1 Corinthians 6:11).

hard.q: Does verse 22 forbid all sexual relationships between men, and does it still apply to Christians?
hard.a:
Jewish and Christian traditions have historically read verse 22 as forbidding sexual relations between men, and most Christian interpreters have seen it as grounded in the creation pattern of male and female in Genesis 1 and 2, not only in Israel's purity system. They note that the verse sits among laws Christians still regard as binding (against incest, adultery, and child sacrifice), and that the Greek word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 6:9 and 1 Timothy 1:10 appears to be formed from the wording of this verse and Leviticus 20:13 in the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation. This remains the teaching of the Catholic and Orthodox churches and most Protestant churches worldwide.

Other interpreters, especially in some Western Protestant churches since the late twentieth century, argue that the verse addresses particular ancient practices, such as sex tied to pagan worship, exploitative relations, or a concern about a man being treated as a woman in a patriarchal order, and that it did not have in view committed same-sex partnerships. Some add that Christians already set aside other Holiness Code rules, such as the ban on mixed fabrics in 19:19. Traditional interpreters respond that the New Testament reaffirms the sexual laws while setting aside food and purity laws. The question divides churches today, and readers should know both the historic reading and the arguments made against it.

questions: Israel was told to be unlike both the land it came from and the land it was going to. What customs of your own culture do you absorb without noticing?
Many of these laws protect the most vulnerable people in a household. How does this change the way you think about sexual ethics as a matter of justice and care, not only rules?
Verse 5 presents God's statutes as the way to life. Where have you experienced God's commands as restrictions, and where as the shape of a good life?
